title: 1Up USA Recon Rack and RakAttach: A Long Term Review – Paul Kalifatidi
content:
1Up USA makes all of its bike racks in Dickeyville, Wisconsin, including its vertical carry Recon Rack. These racks and accessories are known for superior build quality, durability, and repairability, so it’s not often that they need to update their designs. In 2024, 1Up released an update to the Recon Rack, a vertical carry rack designed to haul several bikes. For the past year, Paul has been using one in combination with the RakAttach hitch receiver swing-out. Follow along for his review of the mk. 2 Recon Rack and mk.3 RakAttach from 1Up USA.

The vertical carry rack is a mainstay in my home in Bellingham, WA. We have a ton of families that ride bikes and regularly need to carry four or more bicycles. Lots of people also have them just to cut down on the number of cars needed to get everyone and their bikes to the trailhead. If there’s anything all cyclists can agree on, it’s fewer cars on the road.

I have been using the 1Up USA Recon Rack mk.2 in conjunction with their RakAttach mk.3 swing-out receiver since last August. Like all of their products, I have mostly great things to say, with a few caveats. Follow along for my review.

1Up Recon Rack mk. 2 Quick Hits

  • Full bolt-together design
  • Blend of aluminum and steel components for a high strength-to-weight ratio
  • Pivoting design makes for easy loading
  • Off-road rated with included stability straps
  • Anti-wobble design eliminates play between the rack and receiver
  • Clearance for 24” to 32” wheels, up to 5” wide, max 56″ wheelbase
  • Available in 4, 5, and 6 bike configurations
  • Rack weight:
    • Recon 4: 72 lbs
    • Recon 5: 80 lbs
    • Recon 6: 87 lbs
  • Carrying capacity: 45 lbs per basket
  • 2″ receiver only
  • Compatible with APS panel accessories
  • Made in WI, USA with lifetime warranty

I Like Bike Racks

I like cars. That’s a crazy start to an article in this publication, I know – let me explain. I like the tool that is a car; being able to transport myself, many of my friends, belongings, and hobbies across great distances while simultaneously getting to know a machine that feels more alive than just a lump of metal is a wonderful hobby. It’s why I write Radical Rigs, a series supported by 1Up USA.

Even though I love cars, I rarely drive. In my day-to-day life, I tend to drive my car maybe once a week. I hate cars and how much of our world we’ve handed over to parking lots, pedestrian-unfriendly infrastructure, and the isolating convenience of metal cages. This is a complex issue, but I love a classic American road trip with bikes. We live in a beautiful world. I think the bike rack helps us see more of it.

I don’t have time or energy for janky bike racks made of plastic parts and poor design, so I’ve always been drawn to 1Up USA’s durable and utilitarian design. Let’s get into my review.

1Up Recon Rack Assembly

The Recon Rack arrives in a few boxes. Assembly took me about an hour and was fairly straightforward. I thought I could do it on intuition, but my advice is to set ego aside and simply follow the instructions. They just work.

If you can work on bikes, you can assemble this rack. One issue with the Recon Rack’s easily assembled, repairable design is the number of fasteners that can vibrate loose. The Recon 4 has many bolts. While I have yet to find any that have shaken themselves free, I have found two that became finger-tight loose over time.

Since going through a second time and giving all of the bolts and nylock nuts a second torque, I have had no issues. I have gotten into the habit of occasionally checking them when I have my socket wrench on hand during other car maintenance duties. I don’t think this is a bad design, as I’d much prefer being able to rebuild something with nuts and bolts rather than a torch and a welder.

1Up Recon Durability, Repairability, and Build Quality

The repairability and the durability of any piece of equipment are perhaps the most important criteria I consider when choosing a product. This is why I have always been drawn to 1Up’s racks. Their platform racks are the most durable on the market. I have seen the plastic parts on other brands’ racks slowly disintegrate, while 1Up’s fading anodized finish seems to be the only sign of age. Not only are their platform racks long-lasting, but they are repairable with simple tools and an easy-to-use spare parts catalog. I have even Frankensteined a hitch rack out of their roof rack just using their part diagrams.

The rack is burly, as expected for off-road-rated equipment. It is constructed out of a blend of steel and aluminum. The stinger, upright, and horizontal beams are made of steel as they carry the bulk of the load. The baskets and various other brackets are made of aluminum. This saves a considerable amount of weight compared to the previous design. The entire system is anchored into the hitch receiver using a very secure anti-wobble design. A wedge expands inside the receiver to eliminate all play in the system. It works well and creates a stiff platform.

Off-Road Use

1Up supplies two cam straps for off-road use. These tension the top of the rack to the hitch receiver and create a more rigid system. There is noticeably less movement when using the straps. When driving off-road with a bike rack, the biggest issue is dragging the rack over obstacles while the vehicle undulates across an uneven surface. The Recon Rack’s skeleton is a 90-degree bend from the stinger (which enters the hitch receiver) and the upright (which holds the bikes). This rack sticks quite far out of the back of my truck, further accentuated by my use of the RakAttach swingout.

The combination of swingout and long stinger results in a lesser departure angle (the measure of how steep an incline the vehicle can navigate before putting the rack into the ground). I have scraped and banged the rack many times, mostly when crossing small creeks and depressions. Some other vertical racks mitigate this issue by using two 45-degree bends as opposed to one 90-degree bend. That said, the rack is durable, and I haven’t damaged it beyond scratches and gouges.

Loading Bikes

Loading bikes is simple if you are tall and on a level surface. I’m 5’10” and don’t have an issue lifting 35-pound bikes into the baskets. My 5’4″ friend was able to load bikes without lowering the rack, but it wasn’t the easiest for her. If you are shorter or less able, then this might be a challenge, and I recommend lowering the rack halfway. It is easiest to load bikes right to left, like reading, and to remove in the opposite direction. I occasionally ran into the issue of handlebars and top tubes interfering with one another. Unlike the platform racks from 1Up, there isn’t any way to adjust the bikes’ position in relation to one another, so you have to rearrange the order of bikes to make clearance.

Securing Bikes

Once situated, the front wheel rests in the basket and the rear wheel leans into the lower crossbar. Most vertical racks secure bikes at the top of the rack in a basket or by holding the wheel, stem, or fork crown with a strap. There is no strap at the top of the Recon Rack; 1 Up approaches this completely differently. There is a cam strap that goes around the pedal spindle, around a hook, through the rear wheel, and to another hook on the crossbar. This single strap pulls the bike down into the basket and against the lower crossbar. It is quite effective, but I do have my issues with it.

The problem with this system is that the strap can trap slack. While parts of the system might be tight, there could be strapped layers of slack. Once moving, this slack can work itself into the whole system. The result could be catastrophic if the strap manages to jump out of one of the wheel hooks or off the pedal. I found the best way to take up slack in the cam strap is to put the strapped pedal at 6 o’clock and then move it through the pedal stroke. Then I jostle and adjust until I can confirm that there isn’t any slack left to remove. It requires some mindfulness.

These straps are fully removable, meaning that they do not face the elements when not in use. It does mean that they are more easily misplaced, and indeed, I somehow lost two of them. You can order straps from 1Up, but you can also use generic cam straps found at any hardware or outdoor store. I cut some NRS straps that I already had to the proper length and used those.

Recon Rack Bike Compatibility

1Up USA states that the rack is compatible with 24” to 29” wheels up to 5″ wide and wheelbases up to 54″ long. 1Up also sells a kit that adapts the rack to children’s bikes with wheels smaller than 24″. I also have a 32″ bike in for review and it fits just fine in the wheel basket, although 1Up has yet to come out and say that this wheel size is supported by the Recon Rack. They did release a kit that makes their other racks compatible with 32″ wheels, but the Recon has yet to see any official upgrade kit. I suspect that it does not need one. When loading road bikes or gravel bikes, take care not to smack the downtube on the wheel basket.

Tilting the Recon Rack

The mechanism for tilting the rack down requires more fiddling than I feel like it should. There is a pin that locks the rack in the upright position and a lever that actuates a stopper in the hinge. With cold or muddy hands, I have bashed my knuckles while inserting or removing the cotter pin through the hinge. Some play in the sandwiched steel pieces and plastic bushing of the hinge assembly makes it challenging to line up all the holes for the pin. I end up pushing the rack back and forth while wiggling the pin to remove or insert it. This isn’t very challenging when the rack is empty, but when bikes are loaded, it’s far harder.

If you want to lower it all the way down, then there is a second pin that needs to be removed. I rarely messed with that second pin. The rack doesn’t hinge all the way to the ground, and you can’t load bikes with that pin removed, so I don’t quite understand the point. Frankly, the entire tilting mechanism became unnecessary for me, given the use of the swingout and my ability as a 5’10” human to load bikes in the vertical position. So keep that in mind.

Noises

Lastly, I ran into some noises. The most annoying was the intermittent metallic rattle that seemed to come from the latching mechanism actuated by the red lever on the upright portion of the rack. I got rid of it by putting a piece of electrical tape over that lever to dampen things. It works, but it does get in the way of tilting the rack.

There was some pretty severe squealing from the joint after some dusty road tripping. It sounded like a dying dinosaur. I learned the hard way not to add lubricant to the system, as that turned my dying dinosaur into a zombie dinosaur. A neighbor even walked over and asked if I wanted WD-40. I informed him that lubricant only angers the beast. I then proceeded to dismantle the hinge and thoroughly clean it. This vanquished the dinosaur noise. So if it starts to sound like Jurassic Park, don’t lubricate it; just clean it. You don’t even have to do a full disassembly; just move things around with water spraying into the joints.

Pros

  • Easily and securely carries 1-6 bikes, depending on the model you choose
  • Relatively easy to load and unload
  • User-rebuildable design makes replacing damaged parts easy
  • No plastic or fabric left to rot in the elements
  • Rated for off-road use
  • Anti-wobble mechanism works great
  • Compatible with APS panel accessories

Cons

  • Strap system increases odds of human error
  • Lowering rack is quite fiddly with multiple pins and slight tolerance issues
  • Can rattle
  • Severe hang-over makes for poor departure angle

See the Recon Rack at 1Up USA.

1Up RakAttach mk. 3

The 1Up RakAttach name has been in use for a while; 1Up is now on the third generation of their standard swing-out hitch receiver. I have had it for more than a year now and have found all of the parts that shine and those that could be better. And though I don’t think it is 1Up’s finest product, it has been on my truck for over a year without issue.

Quick Hits

  • Swingout Weight: 56 lbs
  • Total Weight Capacity: 275 lbs
  • Receiver Size: 2″
  • Swings out 100 degrees
  • Offroad rated
  • Material: Powder-coated steel
  • Includes Anti-Wobble Bracket and locking hitch pin
  • Compatible with various accessories like APS panel, table, and roof rack adapter bracket
  • Cannot be used for towing

Why a Swingout?

Mostly: practicality. If you have a car like my KZJ95 Prado that has a side-opening trunk, accessing the rear of the vehicle with bikes on a rack is basically a non-starter. Without a swingout, I am constantly holding my trunk to make sure it doesn’t hit my bike rack while shimmying whatever object I’m trying to place or retrieve through the cracked door. Tilting the laden bike rack down won’t drastically change that amount of space I have to work with. On vehicles like Subarus where the trunk opens up, you’ll likely find greater success in getting your trunk fully open, but you still have to dodge handlebars and tires to actually have access to the trunk space. Even with one bike on a rack, tilting it becomes a bit of a cumbersome task. Many? I hope you’re warmed up for your best hang-clean.

Easily the biggest selling point of a swing-out is the unencumbered access to the rear of the vehicle. No longer are you snagging yourself on handlebars or bashing knees on platforms. Truly, it makes the headaches of a bike rack mostly disappear. Additionally, if you are sleeping in your vehicle while camping, it creates a safe, lockable spot for your bikes where they are not in the way of meal prep and aren’t spending a night locked up to a hedge. They are secure, yet out of the way.

What I Like About the RakAttach

The all-steel construction, heavy-duty hardware, and simplicity are confidence-inspiring. 1Up states that this swing-out is off-road rated, and I believe them. It’s built like a tank. I don’t drive like a Hoonigan off-road, but I do bash my rack on rocks every now and then. The RakAttach has held up fine.

It has a weight rating of 275 pounds. Let’s assume you’re loading 35-pound bikes on 1Up’s 47-pound Heavy Duty two-tray platform with two of the add-on platforms for a capacity of four bikes. You’d only be loading the RakAttach with 224 pounds. Impressive. I have the vertical-carry Recon Rack, four-bike capacity, currently mounted. In total, four enduro bikes and the rack add up to 252 pounds; still safe. I don’t need more capacity; I don’t carry any bikes heavier than ~40 pounds and can’t fit more than five riders in my car anyways. So, this system works great for me.

There also isn’t a ton to maintain on this swingout, as one would hope for a piece of hardware that spends its time in the wheel spray of a vehicle. Instead of swiveling on a large and expensive ball bearing, it uses a durable set of bushings that are less likely to develop play and more easily serviceable. After particularly dusty miles, there is a bit of added friction, but this is quickly alleviated with a rinse of water. DO NOT use a lubricant. As with the Recon Rack, lubricant angers the dusty beast. The bushings are not designed with a lubricant in mind, and adding one will further increase the accumulation of contaminants. Overall, this swing-out is durable and reliable.

Underbaked Anti-Wobble

The most obvious and frustrating aspect of the RakAttach is the underbaked anti-wobble mechanism that seems completely out of place on a 1Up product. In most of their products, there is a wedge or ball that forces the stinger into a corner of the receiver, where it won’t move, wobble, or sag. On the RakAttach, there is no such thing.

Instead, the hitch pin is a bolt that threads into a bracket on the inside of the stinger. The goal is to suck the stinger to the side of the receiver, eliminating wobble. In a perfect world, this would work. The issue is that the hitch receiver on my Prado has a weld relatively close to the hitchpin hole. This meant that I had to trim the washer of the hitchpin bolt to clear the weld. Still, this bolt gradually loosened over time and introduced play into the system. There is nothing indexing the stinger in the vertical axis, only the horizontal. I know I’m not alone in this, as I’ve read other reports and reviews stating the same thing: occasionally tightening that bolt is necessary.

I would happily pay a bit more money if 1Up could incorporate the same anti-wobble mechanism in the RakAttach that is in the Recon Rack. I did ask 1Up if that would ever happen, and they responded with a bit of insight into why this system is as it is. The current insert and hitchpin bolt works in any orientation. This is the key to making the flippable design work and allows you to choose the direction in which the RakAttach opens.

Recently, 1Up USA announced the RakAttach XL, an even burlier swingout with a higher carrying capacity of 375 pounds and a much better anti-wobble design similar to the one on the Recon rack. I don’t need a swingout that weighs ~20 pounds more and has a higher weight capacity, but if you do, the XL is going to be a great option.

Operating the Swingout

Most swingouts have redundant systems to prevent catastrophe. On the RakAttach, this is a magnetic pin in the joint that acts as a stopper if the clamping mechanism at the swingout’s center fails. The clamp is the main closure that eliminates play in the system; the pin is the redundancy. The pin also acts as a stopper when the rack is open; there are two holes allowing you to choose half-open or fully-open positions. I added some tic marks with a gold Sharpie so it was easier to see the positions in which the hole align. Was it necessary? No, but I do think it is an easy and free upgrade.

The issue I have with the clamp and pin arrangement is in accessing both of them. If you have a bike on the rack, or something else in the way, like a spare tire and Colfax Design Works QR tire bag, you might still have to walk around to both sides to remove the pin, then undo the clamp. Otherwise you get stuck in this awkward position of trying to manipulate them from a single side while crawling under whatever obstruction is in the way. I did eventually get used to the workflow. It’s a small concession for such flexibility.

Another minor issue is that this pin is magnetic, and accumulates magnetic debris or traps sand underneath it. This has worn away at the powdercoat and resulted in small amounts of rust. It’s nothing a little bit of cleaning and paint can’t fix, but still, it feels like a slightly overengineered solution that introduced a new issue. That is generally how I feel about putting magnets in strange places.

RakAttach Accessories

The RakAttach offers some optional add-on features. I purchased the traction bar upgrade that bolts to the top of the swing-out to offer a bit more purchase in wet or muddy conditions. It’s great for crawling onto my bed platform or accessing the top of my car for cleaning or roof-mounted accessories. It’s a more durable solution than grip tape, but admittedly more expensive. Another optional accessory would be 1Up’s APS MOLLE panel, which adds options for any MOLLE-compatible gear that you might want to carry (like jerry cans, traction boards, etc). Most interesting, at least to me, would be adding the folding table upgrade to this system. There is also a bracket that you can add to adapt a 1Up roof rack to the swingout, if you have a roof rack and want to increase the total bike holding capacity of this system.

TL;DR

Long story short: I like this product, even with its downsides. It’s not perfect, but it works. It gets the bike rack out of the way while being burly and adaptable. The anti-wobble mechanism needs attention once in a while, but this is because the swingout can be flipped in either direction. This is a great swingout if your hitch receiver has ample clearance around the hitchpin hole and you need to carry up to 275 pounds of gear/bikes.

Pros

  • Super burly design is confidence-inspiring
  • Designed to open in either direction
  • Compatible with APS MOLLE panel accessories
  • Weight capacity of 275 pounds
  • Offroad rated

Cons

  • Anti-wobble mechanism does not work well
  • Design requires access to both ends of the rack
  • Magnetic pin accumulates debris and damages powdercoat

See the RakAttach at 1Up USA.
